How to Cut PMMA with a CNC Machine? Surface Finishes for CNC Acrylic Where is CNC Machined Acrylic Used? FAQs Acrylic (PMMA) has become one of those go-to materials you're probably seeing everywhere now.. Signage, product displays, prototypes, even precision optical housings. People choose it because it looks like glass but weighs half as much, it won't shatter the way glass does, and when it's machined properly it stays clearer than polycarbonate. That said, machining acrylic is tricky . Push the feeds too hard and you'll melt the surface. Run a dull tool and you'll get chips, cracks, or stress marks. Even when the part looks good on the outside, the wrong cutting path or coolant setup can leave hidden stresses inside the material. This is exactly why CNC acrylic machining makes such a difference. A CNC can hold micron-level accuracy, leave polished edges, and give you surface finishes that look molded, not hacked together. It scales, too, whether you need a one-off prototype or a batch of production-ready pieces. See why acrylic is best if it's CNC machined? At JLCCNC , we use these same methods on our own shop floor. And because we've streamlined the process for many years now, our CNC acrylic machining services start at just $1 per part , making it easy to take a clear idea and turn it into a clear, professional-grade part. What Makes Acrylic (PMMA) Unique? (Istock) Compared to other common plastics, acrylic (PMMA) brings a very different set of strengths to the table. ABS is tough and impact-resistant, but it's opaque and doesn't have the clarity designers often need. Polycarbonate is almost unbreakable, but it scratches easily and tends to yellow over time. Acrylic sits right in the middle: it offers glass-like transparency , good surface hardness, and a glossy finish that makes it the material of choice for displays, housings, and optical parts. That said, acrylic is also more brittle than ABS or polycarbonate. Push it too hard and it will chip or crack. The upside is that when machining acrylic is done correctly, sharp tools, right speeds, and proper fixturing, it rewards you with parts that look polished straight off the machine. This is also why CNC acrylic machining is often a better option than laser cutting. Laser cutting can be fast, but it leaves burned edges and micro-cracks that weaken the part and ruin the clarity. A CNC, on the other hand, can cut cleanly, hold tolerances, and even create features like tapped holes or complex geometries that a laser simply can't manage. How to Cut PMMA with a CNC Machine? (Istock) CNC machining acrylic isn't just about pressing start on a machine, it's a carefully staged process that determines whether you end up with a crystal-clear, precision part… or a cloudy, cracked mess. Here's how the process is done right: 1. CAD Design & Preparation Everything starts with a digital blueprint. A CAD model defines every curve, hole, and pocket of the part. For acrylic, designers often add radiused corners and avoid stress risers that could cause cracking during machining. 2. Choosing the Right Acrylic Not all acrylic is created equal. Cast acrylic machines beautifully and yields optical-grade edges, while extruded acrylic is cheaper but prone to gumming and stress marks. Knowing the difference can improve your results. 3. Machine Setup & Calibration Acrylic is unforgiving if your machine isn't dialed in. Calibration includes spindle runout checks, tool offsetting, and ensuring coolant or air-assist systems are clean and ready to prevent heat buildup. 4. Tool Selection Sharp, single-flute or polished-flute end mills are the go-to for acrylic. They evacuate chips cleanly and minimize friction that causes melting. Dull tools? Instant haze and chatter lines. 5. Workholding Strategy Thin sheets can flex like a drum skin. Vacuum tables, sacrificial backers, or low-profile clamps are used to keep the material stable. Weak or unstable workholding nearly always leads to chipped edges or distorted cuts. 6. Programming Feeds & Speeds This is where acrylic separates pros from amateurs. Too fast and you melt. Too slow and you chip. Ideal spindle speeds are high (often 15,000-20,000 RPM) with lighter passes and air blast cooling. CAM software translates the CAD model into G-code tuned for acrylic's quirks. 7. Test Cut & Fine-Tuning Smart machinists don't dive straight into the final part. A quick test cut on scrap material helps validate parameters and surface finish before committing to the real job. 8. Machining the Part With everything locked in, the CNC runs its programmed path, peeling away material to reveal a polished, precise acrylic part. Done right, the edges are clear, burr-free, and ready for assembly or finishing. Pro tip: These steps take years of shop-floor trial-and-error to master. At JLCCNC, we shortcut that process, our CNC acrylic machining services are optimized for optical-grade finishes , starting at just $1 per part , with online quoting and global shipping. And the best part is, you can get a free quote today ! Design Tips for Acrylic CNC Machining (Istock) Acrylic rewards good design, but punishes careless ones. If you want crystal-clear results without cracking, here are a few proven tips from our machining floor: 1. Respect Minimum Wall Thickness Acrylic is brittle compared to ABS or nylon. Go too thin and you'll get stress fractures during machining or assembly. As a rule of thumb, keep wall thickness above 1.5-2 mm for structural parts. Thicker walls are even better if the part will be drilled, tapped, or fastened later. 2. Round Those Internal Corners Sharp 90° corners look good on CAD but act like stress concentrators in acrylic. Adding a fillet radius (ideally matching your end mill size) not only improves strength but also reduces machining chatter and tool wear. 3. Know When to Engrave vs. Cut Through For lettering, logos, or scale markings, engraving is cleaner and keeps the part intact. Through-cuts look sleek, but they risk edge chipping and require careful workholding. We often recommend engraving for functional labels and through-cuts for design features. 4. Tolerances You Can Expect With CNC acrylic machining, JLCCNC typically achieves ±0.05 mm tolerances on critical dimensions . Optical-grade edges are possible without post-polishing, though certain high-clarity applications may benefit from flame or vapor finishing after machining. Surface Finishes for CNC Acrylic (Istock) Not every acrylic part needs to look like it belongs in a museum, but when it does, finish matters. CNC machining alone leaves a smooth but slightly frosted surface. For true optical clarity, secondary finishing comes into play: Finish Type Process Result Best For As-Machined Directly off the CNC, no extra steps Matte/satin look, minor tool marks visible Functional covers, jigs, non-visual parts Flame Polished Torch was briefly applied to edges Glossy, glass-like edge finish Displays, luxury products, signage Vapor Polished Solvent vapor melts the surface layer Optical clarity, near-invisible tool paths Lenses, light guides, medical devices When to use polishing : If the part interacts with light (optics, displays, transparent prototypes), flame or vapor polishing is a must. For mechanical housings or machine guards, an as-machined surface is often more than enough. CNC Acrylic Service vs. DIY Cutting Could you cut acrylic in your shop? Sure. Should you? Depends. Why outsource to a CNC acrylic service: Accuracy & repeatability: Tolerances down to ±0.05 mm, impossible with a jigsaw or drill press. Polished finish: Skip the hours of hand-sanding. No tooling investment: End mills for acrylic aren't cheap, and mistakes cost even more. Speed: Upload your CAD file, get finished parts in days. JLCCNC's acrylic CNC services save time and deliver client-ready clarity from the start. When DIY cutting makes sense: Flat, simple 2D shapes (panels, covers). Hobby projects where clarity isn't critical. Quick one-off mockups before committing to professional machining. Where is CNC Machined Acrylic Used? (Istock) Acrylic's mix of transparency and machinability makes it a favorite in industries where looks and function meet: Signage & Display Panels : Retail, trade shows, art installations. Protective Covers & Machine Guards : Durable, shatter-resistant safety shields. Medical & Lab Equipment : Chambers, trays, and housings that demand clarity. Prototypes for Consumer Products : Transparent housings, industrial design models. FAQs Can CNC cut acrylic better than laser cutting? Yes. CNC produces smoother edges, tighter tolerances, and avoids the heat distortion that laser cutting can cause. What's the best tool for machining acrylic? Single-flute carbide end mills are ideal, they eject chips cleanly and reduce heat buildup. How do you prevent acrylic from melting during cutting? Proper feeds/speeds, sharp tooling, and coolant application keep friction under control. What surface finishes are possible with CNC acrylic machining? As-machined, flame polished, and vapor polished finishes, from matte functional to optical-grade clarity. Is CNC acrylic machining cost-effective for prototypes? Yes, especially when you factor in precision, clarity, and reduced rework. JLCCNC offers services starting at just $1 per part. Conclusion CNC acrylic machining turns a brittle, transparent material into everything from trade show displays to precision lab components. The key is experience: without the right feeds, tools, and finishing, you risk cracks, haze, or worse, scrap. Need CNC acrylic cutting services? JLCCNC offers professional machining from $1 per part.
